summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It plays with the large size of IPv6 addresses, suggesting new and "innovative" address schemes for security and cloud computing. Do not take it as a real design. It is marked experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8135 is an April 1st joke about changing IPv6 addresses into complex numbers. It assigns real and imaginary parts to addresses and uses mathematical terms for a series of playful address types.

subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing complex-number IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke presents fixed integer addresses as a poor fit for mobile and virtual devices.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes representing a 128-bit IPv6 address as two 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point values, one real and one imaginary.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8135 is an Experimental joke document, not a real IPv6 addressing specification.

today: RFC 8135 is Experimental and dated April 1, 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Complex Addressing Idea
sections.content: RFC 8135 is an April 1st joke proposing complex addressing in IPv6. It presents traditional IP addresses as integer values and suggests using floating-point and complex numbers instead. Its proposal divides a 128-bit IPv6 address into a real part and an imaginary part.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke proposes treating an IPv6 address as a complex number. The address has a real part and an imaginary part.

sections.title: Real, Imaginary, and Other Addresses
sections.content: The RFC describes a real address as identifying a device's real location and an imaginary address as representing another possible location. It also introduces floating, flying, prime, composite, safe, rational, irrational, and geometric address categories. These sections apply mathematical terms to networking in the document's deliberately playful proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The document invents address categories using mathematical words such as real, imaginary, prime, and polar. These names are part of its joke proposal.

sections.title: Mapping the Address Bits
sections.content: The proposed mapping divides the 128-bit IPv6 address into two 64-bit halves. The upper half holds the real part, while the lower half holds the imaginary part. Both parts are represented as 64-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 format.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed address uses one 64-bit half for the real part and one 64-bit half for the imaginary part. The RFC specifies IEEE 754 floating-point representation for each half.
